name: Proxmox VE
summary: Open-source enterprise virtualisation and containerisation platform based on Debian GNU/Linux, combining the KVM hypervisor, LXC containers, the pmxcfs distributed cluster file system and Ceph/ZFS storage under a unified web interface.
license: GNU AGPLv3 (Affero General Public License v3)

content.introduction: Proxmox VE (Proxmox Virtual Environment) is a complete open-source enterprise virtualisation software solution developed by the Austrian company Proxmox Server Solutions GmbH. Designed to simplify the management of data centres and virtualised computing infrastructures, it combines two major virtualisation technologies, the KVM hypervisor and LXC system containers, within a unified web administration interface.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Proxmox VE is installed on standard x86-64 hardware as a specialised distribution resting on the Debian GNU/Linux foundation. It integrates a custom Linux kernel maintained by Proxmox (following the LTS branches of the upstream Ubuntu/Linux kernel), optimised with the necessary hardware drivers and native support for OpenZFS, Ceph and KVM virtualisation. The platform turns individual physical servers into computing and storage nodes capable of operating autonomously or grouped into high-availability clusters.
content.dual_virtualization_kvm_and_lxc: One of the architectural foundations of Proxmox VE lies in its technological duality. For the execution of heterogeneous guest operating systems (Microsoft Windows, various Linux distributions, BSD systems), Proxmox VE uses the QEMU/KVM hypervisor with assisted hardware virtualisation (Intel VT-x and AMD-V) and support for direct PCI device passthrough (PCIe passthrough). For Linux workloads requiring maximum I/O performance and a low memory footprint, the platform offers LXC system containers (Linux Containers), which share the host kernel without an intermediate emulation layer.
content.clustering_and_cluster_filesystem_pmxcfs: Cluster management in Proxmox VE adopts a decentralised multi-master architecture without a single dedicated management node. This coordination rests on the exclusive pmxcfs file system (Proxmox Cluster File System). Designed as an SQLite database persisted on disk and replicated in RAM (up to 128 MB), pmxcfs synchronises in real time the configuration of thousands of virtual machines and containers on all the nodes of the cluster through the Corosync messaging and quorum engine (Totem protocol). Any connected node can thus drive the whole cluster without risk of a single point of failure (SPOF).
content.storage_integration_ceph_zfs_and_backup: Proxmox VE offers in-depth native support for local and distributed storage architectures. It directly integrates OpenZFS management for resilient local storage (RAIDZ, mirrors, snapshots and scheduled asynchronous replication) as well as LVM-thin. At cluster scale, Proxmox VE integrates a complete distributed storage management stack for Ceph (MON, MGR, OSD and MDS metadata servers), administrable directly from the web interface to provide RBD block storage and shared CephFS file systems. The solution also interfaces natively with Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) to run incremental backups, deduplicated at the source and encrypted on the client side.
content.management_interface_and_rest_api: Day-to-day administration is carried out entirely through a secure HTTPS web graphical interface based on ExtJS, without requiring a heavy agent on client machines. The interface offers live monitoring of hardware resources, software network management (SDN, VLANs, Linux bridges, Open vSwitch), configuration of the integrated firewall per machine or at cluster scale, and the HTML5 graphical console (noVNC or SPICE). All actions are relayed by a complete RESTful API exposed by the background services, making the platform fully automatable through command-line scripts (`pvesh`), Terraform, Ansible or Packer.
content.release_history_9_2: Version 9.2 was released on 21 May 2026. It rests on Debian Trixie (13.5), with the Linux 7.0 kernel as the default stable version, QEMU 11.0, LXC 7.0, ZFS 2.4 and Ceph Squid 19.2.3 or Tentacle 20.2.1. The official roadmap associates it with the dynamic load balancing of the Cluster Resource Scheduler. The arm64 version, published on 5 August 2026, relies on Debian Trixie 13.6 and Ceph Tentacle 20.2.3.
content.arm64_port_and_limits: Proxmox VE 9.2 for arm64 is the first publication of the product for an architecture other than x86-64. It is fully supported on the NVIDIA Grace and NVIDIA Vera enterprise platforms, and on other ARMv9-A or more recent hardware compatible with UEFI under "best effort" support. Hosts must boot in UEFI and describe their hardware through ACPI: device-tree boards such as the Raspberry Pi are not supported. Some x86 features are absent, including SeaBIOS for virtual machines, AMD SEV and Intel GVT-g; live migration is possible only between nodes of the same architecture. The repositories, the tools and the release cycle are common to both architectures.
content.installation_and_update_paths: Installation is done from an ISO image burned to USB or CD-ROM, or on an existing Debian installation converted for the purpose. System updates come from the package repositories; the wiki recommends applying them frequently in order to receive security fixes and new features. Major version upgrades are documented by a dedicated guide, for example from 8 to 9, and a table of supported versions indicates the current version and the end-of-life date of earlier versions.
content.cluster_resource_scheduler: The Cluster Resource Scheduler (CRS) handles load balancing of the cluster. In its dynamic mode, it uses the real-time usage metrics of nodes and guests to distribute the guests managed by the high-availability manager, and can migrate them automatically in order to reduce the overall imbalance between nodes. The behaviour and sensitivity of the mechanism are configurable. This feature appears among the novelties highlighted by the roadmap of version 9.2.
content.documentation_and_support: The reference documentation is the official wiki of the project, which groups the administration documentation, the installation and migration guides, the version roadmap and the support tables. Release announcements refer to the project forum. The source code is spread over the public Proxmox repositories, and technical exchanges go through the mailing list and the forum cited by the project.
content.container_security_and_access_control: The administration guide states the isolation boundary explicitly: containers share the host kernel, which exposes an attack surface, and full virtual machines provide better isolation when containers are offered to untrusted users. LXC compensates with AppArmor profiles that restrict dangerous actions such as mount, with control groups that organise processes hierarchically, and with kernel namespaces; disabling AppArmor for a container by setting `lxc.apparmor.profile = unconfined` is documented as not recommended for production, since misconfiguration or a kernel flaw can then allow privilege escalation inside the guest. Access to the management layer is separated from the guest layer: authentication realms can be local, Microsoft AD or LDAP, permissions are role-based on every object - virtual machines, storage and nodes - and two-factor authentication is available through OATH and YubiKey.
content.debian_base_and_proxmox_kernel: Proxmox VE is a Debian GNU/Linux system with additional repositories that carry the Proxmox packages, so the Debian archive remains available in full, including its security updates and bug fixes, alongside the project's own packages. The kernel is not the stock Debian one: Proxmox builds its own Linux kernel from an Ubuntu kernel base and enables the virtualisation and container features the platform expects, which is why kernel upgrades arrive through the Proxmox repositories and not from the distribution the system was installed from. The install ISO contains a complete Debian system plus the Proxmox packages, and the support table in the FAQ maps each Proxmox VE release to the Debian release it builds on.
advantages: Fully open-source software solution under the strict GNU AGPLv3 licence, without features reserved for closed versions.
High-performance virtualisation duality: complete KVM hypervisor for total isolation and lightweight LXC containers for computing density.
Multi-master cluster architecture without a single central controller thanks to the replicated pmxcfs file system and Corosync.
Native built-in support for the OpenZFS and Ceph enterprise storage technologies directly in the web interface.
Live migration without service interruption of KVM virtual machines and LXC containers between cluster nodes.
Exhaustive RESTful API and native integration with Proxmox Backup Server for deduplicated incremental backup.
disadvantages: The business model reserves the highly stabilised production package repository (Enterprise Repository) and professional support for paid subscriptions.
Demanding learning curve for the optimal configuration of Corosync quorum parameters, Ceph storage and SDN networks.
High sensitivity of Corosync to network latency variations, imperatively requiring a dedicated physical network for cluster communications.
Official support limited to the x86-64 processor architecture for enterprise production environments.
Native backup management without PBS more basic in terms of speed and retention volume.
who_is_it_for: System administrators and enterprise infrastructure teams looking for a proven open-source alternative to proprietary virtualisation suites (VMware vSphere, Nutanix, Hyper-V).
Hosting companies, managed service providers and telecom operators deploying high-availability virtualisation and container clusters.
DevOps teams requiring a unified platform that can be scripted through API to instantiate test, integration and production environments.
Computing enthusiasts and homelab professionals managing versatile personal servers with ZFS storage and LXC containers.
who_is_it_not_for: Beginner users looking for a simple desktop hypervisor to test a system occasionally (VirtualBox or VMware Workstation being better suited).
Infrastructures relying exclusively on ARM64 or RISC-V processors in commercial production without official support from the publisher.
Organisations requiring 24/7 commercial telephone support without being willing to subscribe to a maintenance contract with the publisher.
Microservices environments requiring native Kubernetes orchestration without an underlying hypervisor layer.
content.verdict: Proxmox VE is an open-source virtualisation and private cloud platform. Built on Debian and the KVM hypervisor, it stands out through its multi-master architecture (pmxcfs), its integration of Ceph and ZFS, and its web administration console, for data centres as well as laboratory environments.
